AI adoption

Your team finished the AI training. What happens on Monday?

Turn a learning session into a repeatable workplace habit with one task, one owner and a clear check.

Anzolo Kpazhi Hope15 November 2026 · 2 min read

The training was lively. Your team tried a few prompts, asked good questions and left excited. On Monday, the old spreadsheet returns. By Friday, nobody can explain what changed.

If you have organised a session like that, do not assume your team is uninterested. The missing piece may be the bridge between the demonstration and the work waiting on their desks. I would build that bridge before planning the next workshop.

Bring one real task into the room

Choose a task people already recognise: preparing a quotation, organising a customer enquiry or drafting a lesson outline. Use synthetic or properly authorised information. Describe the input, the expected result and the person who checks it.

Let participants see an imperfect output. Ask them to identify what is missing and correct it. A training session that only shows successful results teaches confidence more readily than competence.

Leave with a working routine

For the selected task, write a short routine: when to use AI, what information to provide, what information to exclude and how to review the answer. Put that routine where the team already looks for instructions.

Name a person who can answer questions after the session. Make it acceptable to escalate a confusing case. Without that route, people may either abandon the tool or use it in ways you never intended.

Connect learning to responsibility

My earlier work through GlemVNT received attention for its business and education relationships. I value those relationships because access to a tool and the confidence to use it are different things. The same principle guides how I think about adoption through ECHUKU today.

For a school, that could mean a teacher reviewing a draft before using it with students. For a small business, it could mean a manager approving a customer promise. The useful workflow depends on the setting; the responsibility should remain visible.

Check what survived

A week later, ask each participant to show one completed task. What helped? What needed correction? Was the result better, faster or simply different? Compare similar tasks and record the limitations before claiming a productivity improvement.

You can begin with three people and one workflow. If they can explain the process, use it safely and help a colleague understand it, you have something worth expanding. That is a stronger outcome than a room full of people who briefly enjoyed a demonstration.

Your next step

Before your next workshop, write the Monday-morning task participants should be able to complete and the check that makes it safe.
